extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and advanced undergraduates studying algebraic geometry (readers of Vakil's 'The Rising Sea')
extracted.subtask_description: Chapter excerpts and exercises from a graduate-level algebraic geometry textbook (Vakil). Contains definitions, theorems, proof sketches, and exercises about generic freeness, Chevalley, elimination theory, closed embeddings, projective geometry, Veronese/Veronese embeddings, and related constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 7.4.I Exercise — eventual isomorphism ψn
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming the ascending chain condition on M1, show that for n ≫ 0, ψn is an isomorphism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hint: use the ascending chain condition on M1. (Context: this continues the proof of Generic Freeness.)

rubrics_metrics.name: 7.4.J Exercise — existence of nonzero f making quotients free
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that there is a nonzero f ∈ B such that (Mi+1/Mi)_f is free as a B_f-module for all i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hint: as i varies, Mi+1/Mi passes through only finitely many isomorphism classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: 7.4.K Exercise — union of submodules with free successive quotients is free
rubrics_metrics.description: If M is a B-module that is an increasing union of submodules Mi (M0 = 0) and every Mi+1/Mi is free, show that M is free (no Noetherian hypotheses required).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hint: first construct compatible isomorphisms φn : ⊕_{i=0}^{n-1} Mi+1/Mi → Mn by induction on n. Then show that the colimit φ := lim φn is an isomorphism. More generally, if the Mi+1/Mi are projective modules then M is (non-naturally) isomorphic to their direct sum.

rubrics_metrics.name: 7.4.L Exercise — generic behavior of image of finite-type morphism
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose π : X → Y is a finite type morphism of Noetherian schemes and Y is irreducible. Show there is a dense open subset U ⊂ Y such that the image of π either contains U or is disjoint from U.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hint: reduce to Spec B; by the Generic Freeness Lemma there is nonzero f ∈ B such that A_f is a free B_f-module. It must have zero rank or positive rank; in the first case the image is disjoint from D(f), in the second it contains D(f).

rubrics_metrics.name: 7.4.M Exercise — reduction for Chevalley's Theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that to prove Chevalley’s Theorem it suffices to prove that if π : X → Y is a finite type morphism of Noetherian schemes, then the image of π is constructible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a reduction step toward Chevalley; use prior lemmas such as Generic Freeness and the affineness reductions that follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: 7.4.N Exercise — affine reduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce further (in proving Chevalley) to the case where Y is affine (Y = Spec B), and further reduce to the case where X is affine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard localization/reduction to affines to make the argument algebraic.

rubrics_metrics.name: 7.4.O Exercise — complete Chevalley's Theorem proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Complete the proof of Chevalley’s Theorem 7.4.2 by making the sketched Noetherian induction argument precise (using Exercise 7.4.L and reductions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the 'wave-hands' proof given: deal with components, use irreducibility of Y, apply Exercise 7.4.L to find dense open U where image either contains or is disjoint; if U ≠ Y, induct on complement.

rubrics_metrics.name: 7.4.P Exercise — elimination of quantifiers over algebraically closed field
rubrics_metrics.description: Fix an algebraically closed field k. Given f1,...,fp and g1,...,gq in k[W1,...,Wm,X1,...,Xn], show there is a Zariski-constructible subset Y ⊂ k^m such that for w∈k^m there exists x∈k^n satisfying f1=...=fp=0 and g1≠0,...,gq≠0 if and only if w ∈ Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hints: view the system as defining a locally closed subset X ⊂ A^{m+n}, consider the projection π_cl: X_cl → A^m_cl. Use Chevalley’s Theorem to show image is constructible and Nullstellensatz to relate closed points; this is 'elimination of the ∃ quantifier.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental Theorem of Elimination Theory (7.4.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: The morphism π : P^n_A → Spec A is closed (i.e., sends closed sets to closed sets). No Noetherian hypotheses are required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof proceeds by expressing a closed subset Z ⊂ P^n_A by homogeneous equations and translating the condition 'these equations have a common zero in Proj κ(p)[x0,...,xn]' into vanishing of finitely many determinants (linear algebra argument). See Exercises 7.4.8 and 7.4.Q for completion.

rubrics_metrics.name: 7.4.Q Exercise — complete proof of Elimination Theory theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Complete the proof of the Fundamental Theorem of Elimination Theory 7.4.7 by following the same argument with k replaced by A and gi replaced by fi.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hint: mirror the linear-algebra/determinant argument of 7.4.8 but over the base ring A.

rubrics_metrics.name: 8.1.1 Definition — closed embedding / closed immersion
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π : X → Y is a closed embedding (closed immersion) if it is affine and for every affine open Spec B ⊂ Y with π^{-1}(Spec B) ≅ Spec A, the map B → A is surjective (i.e., A ≅ B/I for some ideal I).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remarks: 'embedding' preferred to 'immersion'; closed subscheme denotes X as a subset of Y when π is inclusion. Locally this models as Spec B/I ⊂ Spec B.

rubrics_metrics.name: 8.1.A Exercise — closed embedding identifies underlying topological space
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that a closed embedding identifies the topological space of X with a closed subset of the topological space of Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cautionary examples: Spec k[x] and Spec k[x]/(x^2) vs Spec k[x]/(x) illustrate that the closed subset alone does not determine the closed subscheme (infinitesimal information lost).

rubrics_metrics.name: 8.1.B Exercise — closed embeddings are finite morphisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that closed embeddings are finite morphisms, hence of finite type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elementary exercise following from the affine description A ≅ B/I.

rubrics_metrics.name: 8.1.C Exercise — composition of closed embeddings
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that the composition of two closed embeddings is a closed embedding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Straightforward via affine local descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 8.1.D Exercise — closed embedding is affine-local on target
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that the property of being a closed embedding is affine-local on the target.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: I.e., can be checked on an affine open cover of Y.

rubrics_metrics.name: 8.1.E Exercise — ideal sheaf from surjection on affines
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is a surjection of rings B → A inducing Spec A → Spec B, show the induced map determines an ideal sheaf I_{X/Y} on Y (kernel of O_Y → π_* O_X), and that it is indeed a sheaf of ideals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recover X from the I(B) on affines; this motivates understanding when collections of ideals on affines glue to a global closed subscheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: 8.1.G Exercise — necessary condition for ideals to define closed subscheme
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose I_{X/Y} is a sheaf of ideals corresponding to a closed embedding X → Y. For an affine open Spec B ⊂ Y and f ∈ B, show that the 'natural map' I(B)_f → I(B_f) is an isomorphism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First state precisely what the 'natural map' is. This necessary condition will be complemented by a sufficiency result (Exercise 8.1.H).

rubrics_metrics.name: 8.1.H Essential Exercise — criterion for ideals on affines to define closed subscheme
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose Y is a scheme and for each affine open Spec B ⊂ Y an ideal I(B) ⊂ B is given such that for each f ∈ B the restriction map induces an isomorphism I(B_f) ≅ I(B)_f. Show these data arise from a unique closed subscheme X → Y (i.e., the Spec B/I(B) glue to a global closed subscheme).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hard exercise; three suggested approaches: (1) check pairwise restrictions on intersections and glue using scheme-gluing; (2) build a sheaf of ideals I and verify its affine sections recover I(B); (3) describe X as a closed subset and define the structure sheaf via compatible germs. This is the precursor to the statement that closed subschemes correspond to quasi-coherent ideal sheaves.

rubrics_metrics.name: 8.1.I Definition/Exercise — vanishing scheme V(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) For s ∈ Γ(Y,O_Y) define the closed subscheme cut out by s, called the vanishing scheme V(s). (b) If u is invertible show V(s)=V(su). (c) For a set S of functions define V(S).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On an affine open Spec B take Spec B/(s|_{Spec B}). Use Exercise 8.1.H to check these local definitions glue to a closed subscheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: 8.1.J Exercise — unions and intersections of closed subschemes; scheme-theoretic behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Define the finite union and arbitrary intersection of closed subschemes of X; (b) describe scheme-theoretic intersection of V(y-x^2) and V(y) in A^2 and interpret multiplicity/nonreducedness; (c) show underlying sets of unions/intersections coincide with set-theoretic unions/intersections in finite cases; (d) describe intersection of V(y^2-x^2) and V(y) and note that scheme-theoretic distributivity may fail (i.e., (X ∪ Y) ∩ Z ≠ (X ∩ Z) ∪ (Y ∩ Z) in general).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hints: in affine case unions correspond to I1 ∩ I2; think about multiplicities and nonreduced structure to see 'fuzz' and intersection multiplicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: 8.1.K Hard Exercise — equivalence of definitions of closed embedding
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that the usual definition (π: X → Y is a homeomorphism onto a closed subset of underlying topological spaces and the induced map π^#: O_Y → π_* O_X is surjective on stalks) agrees with the affine-open surjectivity definition given in 8.1.1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To show surjectivity on stalks from surjectivity on affine opens use that surjectivity of a morphism of sheaves can be checked on a suitable base (Exercise 2.5.E).

rubrics_metrics.name: 8.1.L Exercise — locally closed embeddings locally of finite type
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that locally closed embeddings (i.e., factorizable as a closed embedding followed by an open embedding) are locally of finite type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Easy exercise: follows from properties of closed embeddings and open embeddings.

rubrics_metrics.name: 8.1.M Exercise — equivalences for locally closed subschemes
rubrics_metrics.description: For a morphism V → X consider: (i) V is the intersection of an open subscheme and a closed subscheme; (ii) V is an open subscheme of a closed subscheme (factors open then closed); (iii) V is a closed subscheme of an open subscheme (locally closed embedding). Show (i) and (ii) are equivalent and both imply (iii).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remark: (iii) need not imply (i) or (ii) in pathological cases. Hint: think of the diagram with open/closed embeddings and interpret each condition as existence of parts of this diagram.

rubrics_metrics.name: 8.1.N Exercise — composition of locally closed embeddings
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that the composition of two locally closed embeddings is a locally closed embedding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hint: use implications from Exercise 8.1.M (ii) ⇒ (iii) to structure the factorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: 8.2.1 Example — homogeneous polynomials define closed subschemes in projective space
rubrics_metrics.description: Any homogeneous polynomial f in x0,...,xn defines a closed subscheme of P^n_A (its vanishing scheme). A collection of homogeneous polynomials cuts out a closed subscheme of P^n_A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On the standard affine patches Ui the closed subscheme is given by V(f(x0/i,...,xn/i)); on overlaps the local defining equations agree up to multiplying by a unit (power of x_j/x_i). Exercise 8.2.C shows conversely every closed subscheme of P^n_A arises this way.

rubrics_metrics.name: 8.2.3 Definition — linear space (linear subspace) in projective space
rubrics_metrics.description: The closed subscheme given by an injective linear map V → W induces a closed embedding P(V) → P(W). A linear space of dimension n in P^N is a closed subscheme cut out by N−n k-linearly independent homogeneous linear polynomials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminology: linear space of dimension 1 is a line, of dimension 2 a plane, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: 8.2.G Exercise — Proj of graded ring generated in degree 1 embeds in projective space
rubrics_metrics.description: If S is a finitely generated graded A-algebra generated in degree 1 by x0,...,xn then Proj S can be described as a closed subscheme of P^n_A (via a surjection A[t0,...,tn] → S sending ti ↦ xi).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conclude Proj S ≅ Proj(A[t0,...,tn]/I) and hence is a closed subscheme of some P^n_A; remove degree-1-generation hypothesis later using Exercises 6.4.D and 6.4.G.

rubrics_metrics.name: 8.2.5 Observation — finite morphisms are closed via projectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Second proof that finite morphisms are closed: locally, X is projective over B (Exercise 7.3.J) hence by the Fundamental Theorem of Elimination Theory its image is closed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This uses the interpretation of Proj S as a closed subscheme of projective space when S is generated in degree 1, together with Theorem 7.4.7.

rubrics_metrics.name: 8.2.I Exercise — Veronese subring example (quadratic Veronese)
rubrics_metrics.description: For S = k[x,y], show S_2 ≅ k[u,v,w]/(uw−v^2) via u↦x^2, v↦xy, w↦y^2; interpret Proj S_2 as a conic in P^2 (Veronese embedding).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Exercise 6.4.4 on Veronese subring; this identifies P^1 'in' P^2 as a conic.

rubrics_metrics.name: 8.2.8 Definition — d-uple (Veronese) embedding
rubrics_metrics.description: If S = k[x0,...,xn] then Proj S^{(d)} (the d-th Veronese subring) is the d-uple embedding of P^n into P^{N-1} where N = binom(n+d,d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine previous exercises to see Proj S^{(d)} is a closed embedding; this generalizes the twisted cubic and quadratic Veronese examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: 8.2.J Exercise — rational normal curve via rank conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: With S = k[x,y], show Proj S^{(d)} (the d-uple embedding) is the degree-d rational normal curve in P^N described by the condition that a certain Hankel-like (or catalecticant) matrix has rank 1 (all 2×2 minors vanish).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This extends the twisted cubic case (d=3) and can be seen by expressing degree-d monomials as symmetric tensors; the minors encode the condition of being a pure d-th power.

rubrics_metrics.name: 8.2.L Exercise — equations cutting out the Veronese surface
rubrics_metrics.description: Find six linearly independent quadratic equations vanishing on the Veronese surface Proj S_2 with S = k[x0,x1,x2] (the Veronese surface sits in P^5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hint: use the 3×3 symmetric matrix of pairwise products and the determinant identity det([[x0x0, x0x1, x0x2],[...],[...]]) = 0 to produce relations; you need not show they generate the full ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: 8.2.M Exercise — rulings on the quadric surface
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) For the quadric surface X defined by wz=xy in P^3_k, produce two families of lines parameterized by P^1 and describe them; (b) show through every k-valued point of X there passes one line from each ruling; (c) show there are no other lines on X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct explicit parametric lines [a0 c, b0 c, a0 d, b0 d] as [c,d] varies in P^1; algebraic manipulations (or Bézout in Exercise 8.2.E) show there are only these two rulings. Over algebraically closed fields (char≠2) this gives the two rulings on smooth quadric surfaces.
